sentences.text: The genus Edmontosaurus currently includes two valid species, E. regalis and E. annectens, along with several synonyms such as Anatosaurus, Anatotitan, Claosaurus annectens, and possibly Ugrunaaluk.
Edmontosaurus annectens was one of the largest duck-billed dinosaurs to ever exist, reaching lengths of up to 12 meters and an average weight of 5.6 metric tons.
Its skull was roughly triangular in profile and lacked a bony cranial crest, distinguishing it from many other hadrosaurids.
The brain cavity occupied about a quarter of the skull length and held endocasts ranging from 374 ml to 450 ml.

Exceptionally large specimens measured approximately 15 meters in length and weighed around 15.9 metric tons, while others at the Royal Tyrrell Museum suggest a maximum size of 10 tons or even larger, possibly rivaling Shantungosaurus.
In 2025, researchers detected ancient hydroxyproline in a fossil, confirming the presence of original dinosaur organic material and refuting contamination hypotheses.
In 2003, scientists described evidence of various tumors, including hemangiomas and metastatic cancer, in Edmontosaurus bones.
The Lance Formation preserves two Edmontosaurus "mummies" that provide exceptional preservation of soft tissues.
The genus Edmontosaurus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1917 after the first fossils were discovered in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of southern Alberta.
Specimens for the synonym Claosaurus annectens were collected in 1891 by John Bell Hatcher from the Lance Formation of Wyoming.
In 1942, Lull and Wright created the genus Anatosaurus to classify several hadrosaurid species that did not fit into existing genera.
Edmontosaurus was a large terrestrial herbivore and a facultative biped, primarily moving on four legs but capable of standing or moving on two legs.

Researchers study its diet and physiology by analyzing stable isotopes of carbon and oxygen preserved in tooth enamel, while a 2009 study identified four classes of scratches on teeth indicating complex jaw movements during feeding.
Researchers interpreted skull size correlations as strong evidence that Edmontosaurus skull shape changed dramatically during growth.
Fossils show osteochondrosis, a condition characterized by surficial pits in bones where they articulate.

Computer modeling from 2007 suggests Edmontosaurus could run at speeds up to 45 km/h, though simulations of a kangaroo-like hopping gait indicated a maximum speed of 17.3 m/s, which researchers considered unlikely.
The dinosaur had slim hands with short fingers, rendering its forelimbs ineffective for swimming propulsion.
The top of the tail of the Denver specimen was at least 2.9 meters high, a height only reachable by T. rex from the same rock formation.
Edmontosaurus annectens differs from E. regalis by possessing a longer, lower, and less robust skull.

Edmontosaurus fossils date from the Late Cretaceous, spanning the Campanian to the end of the Maastrichtian stages, with E. regalis found in western North America from rocks dating to 73 million years ago.
The Lance Formation, located approximately 100 km north of Fort Laramie in eastern Wyoming, is interpreted as a bayou setting.
A 2017 study questioned the validity of Ugrunaaluk as a separate genus, suggesting it is indistinguishable from other Edmontosaurus specimens.
There is a debate over whether plant fossils found in an Edmontosaurus specimen represent gut contents or were washed in after death.
